prompt.context: Your client is a gas company that operates in a town with a population of 1,000. There is only one other gas company in this town, and it is 1 mile away. The other nearest gas stations are outside town, and they are 20 miles away (see map exhibit).
prompt.question: The client has been approached by a supermarket with the idea of selling groceries in the gas station. The client is a simple businessman and has hired us to evaluate this proposal. What should our client consider?

clarifying_info.q: What kind of groceries would the gas station sell?
clarifying_info.a: Likely cigarettes, milk, snack foods; probably not fresh produce or healthy foods.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current profitability of the gas station?
clarifying_info.a: The gas station is barely scraping by — profit is essentially 0.

clarifying_info.q: What do we know about the other gas station?
clarifying_info.a: We don't know, but assume they are identical.

exhibits.title: Map of Area
exhibits.shows: A map (not to scale) showing the relative positions of the client gas station, the competitor gas station 1 mile away, and the nearest outside-town stations 20 miles away, within a town of 1,000 people.
exhibits.data: Town population: 1,000; distance between client and competitor: 1 mile; distance to nearest outside-town stations: 20 miles

framework: Revenue: increased grocery sales in-store; increased gas sales by attracting more customers from competitor
Costs: one-time upfront investment (freezers, shelves, utilities); minimal recurring labor cost increase since same staff can handle both
Profit-sharing: any split with the grocery store partner
Competition: what prevents the competitor (station B) from doing the same — prisoner's dilemma dynamic

questions.prompt: What kind of costs could there be?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify one-time capital costs (freezers, shelving, utilities) vs. recurring costs. Key insight: no increase in labor expected because the same staff can handle both gas and groceries.

steps: Investment in freezers, shelves, utilities = $1.25MM total one-time cost
No increase in recurring labor costs

questions.prompt: What are the revenue streams and how large are they? Also calculate the value as a perpetuity.
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify two distinct revenue sources: (1) grocery sales to existing local customers, and (2) incremental gas sales from stealing customers from station B. Key insight: people will not buy MORE gas — the gain is from attracting customers away from the competitor. Then value it as a perpetuity using r=10%, g=0%.

math.setup: Grocery revenue: 500 people x $200/year. Gas revenue: steal 50% of station B's 500 customers (250 people) x $100/year. Perpetuity = total annual cash flow / (r - g)
steps: Town has 1,000 people; each station currently serves ~500 people
Incremental gas sales: steal 50% of station B's 500 customers = 250 people x $100/year = $25,000/year
math.answer: Total annual revenue increase: $125,000/year; perpetuity value: $1.25MM

questions.prompt: What would you advise the gas station owner to do?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize this as a prisoner's dilemma. Strong answers explore all four scenarios: A does it / B responds; A does it / B does not respond; A does not do it / B does it; A does not do it / B does not do it. Push back on whichever scenario the candidate favors to test robustness of reasoning.

brainstorming.prompt: What is keeping the grocery store from also approaching station B with the same proposal?

categories.name: Competitive response risk
ideas: Station B receives the same offer from the grocery store
Station B decides to add groceries independently
If both stations add groceries, incremental gas-customer stealing cancels out
Both stations face the $1.25MM cost with no net revenue gain — could push both out of business

categories.name: First-mover advantage
ideas: Exclusive contract with the grocery store to prevent station B from getting the same offer
Being first to offer groceries may lock in customer loyalty
If station A moves first and station B does not respond, station A can capture all incremental revenue

categories.name: Prisoner's dilemma scenarios
ideas: A acts, B retaliates: value-neutral on revenue but both bear $1.25MM cost — risky
A acts, B does not: A captures $250K revenue benefit and can push B out
A does not act, B acts: A loses $250K in customers, may go out of business
A does not act, B does not act: status quo maintained — both survive at zero profit

recommendation: Option 1: Proceed with adding groceries and attempt to push station B out of business by capturing first-mover advantage
Option 2: Do not proceed and hope station B also refrains — maintaining the status quo
risks: If station A proceeds, station B may retaliate by adding groceries too, leaving both stations with the $1.25MM cost and no net revenue gain
If station A does not proceed, station B may act first, costing station A ~$250K in lost customers and potentially pushing it out of business
next_steps: Negotiate an exclusive contract with the grocery store to prevent them from approaching station B
Conduct due diligence on station B's financial position and likelihood of retaliation
If proceeding, line up financing for the $1.25MM upfront investment before committing
